issues.legal_issue: Whether the arrangement with an occupier amounted to a subletting rather than a licence, and whether consideration could be inferred from the circumstances.
material_facts: A tenant permitted an ice-cream business to operate from a separate portion of the leased commercial premises.
The lower courts found that the ice-cream business had exclusive possession of that portion and rejected the tenant’s explanation for the arrangement as unsatisfactory.
The written agreement described the arrangement as a licence and denied that possession had been transferred, but the landlord was not a party to that agreement.
The evidence included that the ice-cream premises could be locked independently and that the ice-cream business operated separately from the tenant’s business.
issues.conclusion: The transaction was subletting: the evidence supported exclusive possession, and the courts could infer that the arrangement was prompted by monetary consideration despite the absence of direct evidence of rent.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 105 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, a lease transfers a right to enjoy property for consideration; section 52 of the Easements Act distinguishes a licence that creates no interest in the property. Exclusive possession is an important indicator but is not conclusive; the operative intention and substance of the transaction govern, not the label in the agreement. Where a tenant’s explanation is unacceptable after exclusive possession is established, consideration may be inferred from the circumstances and ordinary human conduct. The Court relied on Wood v. Leadbitter, Glenwood Lumber Co. v. Phillips, Associated Hotels of India v. R.N. Kapoor, B.M. Lall v. Dunlop Rubber Co., Qudrat Ullah v. Municipal Board, Bareilly, Board of Revenue v. A.N. Ansari, M.N. Clubwala v. Fida Hussain Saheb, and Dipak Banerjee v. Smt. Lilabati Chakraborty.

predicates.rent_eviction_for_unauthorized_sublettin: A landlord seeks eviction on the ground that a tenant has transferred occupation of part of the premises to another person without authority.
predicates.third_party_exclusive_possession: A third party occupies and controls a distinct part of the premises separately from the tenant.
predicates.tenant_explanation_unacceptable: The tenant’s account of why the third party occupies the premises is rejected as unsatisfactory in light of the evidence.

issues.definition: When an eviction case concerns unauthorized subletting, a third party has exclusive possession, and the tenant’s explanation is unacceptable, the transaction may be treated as subletting for consideration.

issues.legal_issue: Whether a revisional court may replace a concurrent factual finding that is supported by the record with its own assessment of the evidence.
material_facts: The Rent Controller and the appellate authority both found that the ice-cream business had exclusive possession of part of the premises.
The High Court, exercising revision jurisdiction, reappraised the evidence and reversed that concurrent finding.
The High Court relied on plans produced in connection with a separate dispute about structural alterations, although that evidence had not been relied on to rebut exclusive possession.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was not justified in replacing the concurrent finding, which was supported by the evidence, with its own conclusion on an independent reassessment.
issues.legal_principle: The scope of revision depends on the language of the statute conferring it. Even where the revisional power permits examination of the legality or propriety of an order and is wider than the power under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure, revision is not a first or second appeal. A revisional court should be reluctant to reassess evidence and supplant a factual finding where the record supports the finding reached below. Section 15(5) of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949, governed the revisional jurisdiction in this case.

predicates.rent_revision_proceeding: A court is exercising revisional jurisdiction in a rent-control proceeding.
predicates.concurrent_finding_supported_by_record: The courts below reached the same factual finding and evidence in the record supports it.
predicates.revisional_court_reassesses_evidence_ind: The revisional court reassesses the evidence and substitutes a different factual conclusion.

issues.definition: In a rent revision, when a supported concurrent finding is replaced after an independent reassessment, the supported finding should not be displaced in revision.

issues.legal_issue: Whether an appellate court may reverse a trial court’s factual findings based on witnesses’ sensory observations without cogent reasons showing an obvious error.
material_facts: The trial court assessed oral evidence about what witnesses had seen and heard, including evidence concerning the separate operation and possession of the ice-cream business.
The High Court displaced the findings without demonstrating an obvious error in the trial court’s assessment of that evidence.
issues.conclusion: The High Court’s reversal was not justified; an appellate court reversing findings based on perceptive evidence must give cogent reasons showing that the trial court fell into an obvious error.
issues.legal_principle: An appellate court should give weight to a trial judge’s findings based on seeing and hearing witnesses. Where credibility or sensory perception is material, reversal requires cogent reasons demonstrating an obvious error; the appellate court is generally better placed to draw inferences from proved facts when credibility is not in issue. The Court relied on Watt v. Thomas, Benmax v. Austin Motor Co. Ltd., and Sarju Pershad v. Jwaleshwari Pratap Narain Singh.

predicates.appeal_reviewing_trial_fact_findings: An appellate court reviews factual findings made by a trial court.
predicates.finding_depends_on_witness_perception: The finding turns materially on what witnesses perceived or on their credibility as assessed by the trial judge.
predicates.no_cogent_reason_for_obvious_error: The appellate court gives no cogent reason demonstrating an obvious error in the trial court’s assessment.

issues.definition: When an appeal reviews a finding based on witness perception and gives no cogent reason showing obvious error, that finding should not be reversed.

issues.legal_issue: Whether a claim that consideration was not pleaded prevents the court from deciding that a subletting was for consideration when the parties understood and tried that issue.
material_facts: The tenant understood the allegation to include consideration and specifically denied that consideration existed.
The parties presented evidence at trial with knowledge that the nature and consideration of the arrangement were in issue.
issues.conclusion: The objection that consideration had not been pleaded failed; the pleadings were to be construed liberally because the parties understood and tried the issue.
issues.legal_principle: Pleadings should be construed by their substance rather than their form where the parties understood the case and the issues on which they went to trial and produced evidence on them. The Court relied on Ram Sarup Gupta v. Bishun Narain Inter College.

rule.if: rent_eviction_for_unauthorized_subletting and subletting_pleaded and consideration_denied_in_response and parties_tried_consideration_issue

predicates.rent_eviction_for_unauthorized_sublettin: A landlord seeks eviction on the ground that a tenant has sublet premises without authority.
predicates.subletting_pleaded: The landlord pleads that the tenant sublet the premises.
predicates.consideration_denied_in_response: The tenant responds by denying that consideration was given for the alleged transfer of occupation.
predicates.parties_tried_consideration_issue: Both sides understand that consideration is in issue and present evidence on it at trial.

issues.definition: When subletting is pleaded, consideration is denied, and both sides try that issue, the court may decide consideration from the trial record.

issues.legal_issue: Whether the absence of prior notice before appointing a commissioner requires reversal when other evidence supports the finding the commissioner’s report was used to support.
material_facts: The trial court appointed a commissioner to inspect the premises without prior notice to the tenant and did not direct the parties to appear before the commissioner.
The High Court treated the absence of notice as a procedural objection to the commissioner’s report.
Other evidence in the record supported the lower courts’ finding of exclusive possession.
issues.conclusion: The omission in the commissioner’s proceedings did not require reversal because other evidence supported the finding; the Court did not decide whether an ex parte appointment was independently permissible in the circumstances.
issues.legal_principle: Order 26 rule 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure concerns appointment of a commissioner for local investigation. The power to inspect structures may also be referable to Order 39 rule 7, under which notice may be dispensed with if notice would defeat or frustrate the object of the appointment. The Court noted Latchan Naidu v. Rama Krishan Ranga Rao Bahadur Bobbili Samasthanam but expressly left the broader question undecided because other evidence supported the finding.

predicates.rent_eviction_proceeding: A court is deciding an eviction proceeding under rent-control law.
predicates.commissioner_inspection_without_prior_no: A court appoints a commissioner to inspect premises without giving a party prior notice.
predicates.independent_evidence_supports_finding: Evidence apart from the commissioner’s report supports the factual finding at issue.

issues.definition: In an eviction proceeding, an inspection without prior notice does not require reversal when independent evidence supports the relevant finding.
